title: 15.4 A Neuroprosthetic SoC with Sensory Feedback Featuring Frequency-Splitting-Based Wireless Power Transfer with 200Mb/s 0.67pJ/b Backscatter Data Uplink and Unsupervised Multi-Class Spike Sorting
problem: High-channel neural implants enable prosthetic control but lack closed-loop sensory feedback, limiting stability and requiring steep user learning curves. Traditional external feedback introduces latency; electrical stimulation is viable but must reject stimulation artifacts to avoid false feedback loops.
method: Frequency-splitting wireless power transfer delivers power and data on distinct carriers, eliminating cross-talk. Backscatter uplink (200 Mb/s, 0.67 pJ/bit) conveys neural data with minimal power overhead. On-chip unsupervised multi-class spike sorting classifies neural signals locally, reducing data bandwidth. Stimulation artifact rejection circuit prevents positive feedback loops during simultaneous stimulation and recording.

title: SSFT: Algorithm and Hardware Co-design for Structured Sparse Fine-Tuning of Large Language Models
problem: Sparse fine-tuning (SFT) reduces time and memory requirements compared to dense fine-tuning, but GPU implementation underperforms due to irregular sparse data access patterns that modern GPUs cannot efficiently handle, negating computational benefits.
method: SSFT-Alg introduces predictable sparsity patterns reducing memory access overhead and enhancing regularity. SSFT-Hw accelerator optimizes SSFT-Alg with sparsity-aware design avoiding GPU sparse overhead. Co-design balances algorithm structure and hardware capabilities.

title: 3D-TokSIM: Stacking 3D Memory with Token-Stationary Compute-in-Memory for Speculative LLM Inference
problem: LLM autoregressive decoding faces severe memory bandwidth bottleneck from the logic die; 2D memory solutions cannot overcome this due to limited memory-to-logic bandwidth.
method: Proposes 3D-TokSIM combining 3D memory stacking on logic die with token-stationary compute-in-memory (CIM); uses novel token-stationary dataflow to minimize data movement on logic die, reducing power and balancing compute/memory throughput; architecture exploration allocates CIM resources for higher decoding parallelism.

title: DAPPER: A Performance-Attack-Resilient Tracker for RowHammer Defense
problem: Host-side RowHammer mitigation mechanisms rely on shared counter or tracking structures that are vulnerable to Performance Attacks (Perf-Attacks), where adversaries reverse-engineer the shared structure's mapping to artificially inflate DRAM access counters or trigger early resets, degrading performance of co-running benign applications.
method: DAPPER introduces secure hashing to randomize the mapping of DRAM rows to shared tracking structures, preventing adversaries from predicting counter locations. DAPPER-S provides a base secure hashing template using a single hash function. DAPPER-H extends this with double-hashing, novel reset strategies that avoid predictable early resets, and mitigative refresh techniques that piggyback RowHammer mitigations onto scheduled refresh operations to amortize overhead. The combined design uses only 96KB of SRAM per 32GB of DRAM, validated against 57 workloads from SPEC2006, SPEC2017, TPC, Hadoop, MediaBench, and YCSB.

title: Synergistic Die-Level Router for Multi-FPGA System with Time-Division Multiplexing Optimization
problem: Multi-FPGA systems with multiple dies connected via TDM suffer from critical connection delays and routing congestion from super long lines (SLLs) between dies.
method: Die-level router that jointly optimizes routing topology and TDM timing ratios; reduces reliance on SLLs and critical path delays through topology-aware routing decisions.

title: Citadel: Rethinking Memory Allocation to Safeguard Against Inter-Domain Rowhammer Exploits
problem: Rowhammer attacks exploit DRAM's physical row-adjacency to corrupt memory rows belonging to different security domains; hardware mitigations are costly, slow to adopt, and repeatedly circumvented, while software mitigations incur large performance and memory capacity overheads or provide only partial protection.
method: Citadel is a software-based memory allocator that prevents inter-domain Rowhammer by introducing flexible security domains and physically isolating them in disjoint DRAM regions—ensuring no two domains share physically adjacent rows. The allocator tracks DRAM physical row topology and partitions the address space so that domain boundaries are always separated by guard rows or page-aligned gaps. The design supports thousands of simultaneous security domains on server systems with a 7.2% average memory overhead and no measurable performance loss, without requiring hardware changes and remaining deployable on legacy, current, and future DRAM platforms.

title: Device-Aware Test: A Means to Attack Unmodelled Defects (Invited)
problem: Structural testing at advanced technology nodes and for emerging device technologies is insufficient to screen unmodeled defects, resulting in reduced outgoing product quality.
method: Device-Aware Test (DAT) is proposed as a new manufacturing test methodology that goes beyond traditional structural testing by incorporating device-specific models and characteristics to expose unmodeled faults.

title: Zebra: Efficient Redundant Array of Zoned Namespace SSDs Enabled by Zone Random Write Area (ZRWA)
problem: Integrating ZNS SSDs into RAID configurations requires handling partial parity updates (PPUs) that arise from ZNS's append-only write semantics; existing metadata-zone-based solutions become performance bottlenecks under high PPU workloads.
method: Zebra exploits the Zone Random Write Area (ZRWA), the SSD's internal write buffer in front of each zone, to handle PPUs in-place. By ensuring that parity chunks fit within the ZRWA window, Zebra performs partial parity overrides within the buffer rather than writing to separate metadata zones. A set of complementary techniques maintain high performance and reliability across both large-zone and small-zone ZNS SSD models.

title: A 17.7-to-29.5GHz Transceiver Front-End with 3.3dB NF and 20.2dBm OP1dB in 65nm CMOS
problem: Wideband mm-wave transceivers must simultaneously achieve low-noise wideband RX, high-efficiency wideband TX, and excellent TX/RX isolation for 5G, LEO SATCOM, and JSAC applications. These three requirements interact and conflict with conventional designs.
method: The design integrates a wideband RX front-end (3.3dB NF), wideband TX path (20.2dBm OP1dB), and TX/RX isolation circuitry in a single 65nm CMOS process, operating across the 17.7-29.5GHz band via frequency tuning.

title: 20.11 A Crystal-Less BodyID with an Asynchronous Clockless Leakage-Powered Wake-Up Receiver and Over-the-Channel Clock Recovery
problem: Wake-up receivers for ultra-low-power wearables traditionally require always-running clocks and external crystal oscillators for sampling and correlation, consuming unnecessary idle power, adding size/cost, and requiring ULP oscillator with external calibration reference.
method: Asynchronous clockless wake-up receiver design leveraging over-the-channel clock recovery from incoming RF signal to enable direct digital correlation without always-running oscillator, powered by device leakage during idle state, eliminating need for external crystal reference.

title: FlexNeRFer: A Multi-Dataflow, Adaptive Sparsity-Aware Accelerator for On-Device NeRF Rendering
problem: GPUs fail to meet the performance, power, and area requirements for on-device Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) rendering, and existing NeRF-specific accelerators are tuned for a single algorithm, yielding poor efficiency when applied to other NeRF model variants. No hardware exists that efficiently supports the diversity of NeRF frameworks emerging for on-device 3D scene reconstruction.
method: FlexNeRFer combines a flexible Network-on-Chip (NoC) that reconfigures to support multiple dataflow patterns with a precision-scalable MAC array capable of operating at variable bit-widths. The accelerator exploits adaptive sparsity by selecting the optimal sparse tensor storage format at runtime based on the observed sparsity ratio and precision mode, avoiding format-mismatch overhead. The design was validated with a full layout implementation in 28 nm CMOS technology.

title: Chronus: Understanding and Securing the Cutting-Edge Industry Solutions to DRAM Read Disturbance
problem: The DDR5 Per Row Activation Counting (PRAC) RowHammer mitigation introduces non-trivial DRAM access latency overhead (counter increment in critical path) and is vulnerable to the 'wave attack' adversarial pattern, forcing overly conservative refresh thresholds that degrade performance.
method: Chronus is an on-DRAM-die RowHammer mitigation that separates activation counters from data arrays, allowing counter updates to proceed concurrently with data accesses (eliminating the latency penalty). It also dynamically controls the number of preventive refreshes issued per back-off signal to neutralize the wave attack — which forces repeated activation bursts to exhaust a fixed-refresh budget. The mechanism requires only in-DRAM modifications and is open-sourced.

title: A 0.4µW/MHz Reference-Replication-Based RC Oscillator with Path-Delay and Comparator-Offset Cancellation Achieving 9.83ppm/°C from -40 to 125°C
problem: Open-loop RC oscillators struggle with frequency stability against process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) variations due to path-delay and comparator offset sensitivity; closed-loop approaches achieve better stability but incur significant area, power, and circuit complexity overhead.
method: The reference-replication-based RC oscillator cancels path-delay and comparator-offset effects through integrated compensation circuits, achieving ±9.83ppm/°C temperature coefficient across -40 to 125°C while maintaining 0.4µW/MHz power efficiency without switched resistors or polynomial calibration.

title: Data Oblivious CPU: Microarchitectural Side-channel Leakage-Resilient Processor
problem: Microarchitectural side-channel attacks (cache timing, speculative execution) remain broadly applicable despite various targeted defenses; current approaches are narrowly tailored, leaving systems exposed to diverse attack vectors.
method: Dynamic instruction decoding strategy that selectively decodes instructions into secure (side-channel resilient) or performance versions based on the sensitivity of data being processed. Non-sensitive data path uses optimized performance instructions; sensitive data path uses secure variants. Implemented on RISC-V BOOM out-of-order processor.

title: Mithril: A Scalable System for Deep GNN Training
problem: Distributed full-graph deep GNN training does not scale to many layers because inter-GPU communication volume grows with graph size and number of layers, overwhelming existing graph parallelism approaches which partition the graph across GPUs and require massive cross-partition neighbor data exchange.
method: Mithril applies layer-level model parallelism to full-graph GNN training: each GPU owns a disjoint subset of consecutive GNN layers and processes all graph nodes for those layers. This reduces per-epoch communication by a factor equal to the number of GNN layers compared to graph parallelism. Pipeline parallelism across layer-partitioned GPUs is realized by partitioning the graph into dependent chunks; inter-chunk embedding dependencies are broken using embedding speculation (speculative forward pass). A hybrid scheme combines Mithril's layer parallelism with graph parallelism for large graphs to improve GPU utilization and ensure convergence.

title: zkVC: Fast Zero-Knowledge Proof for Private and Verifiable Computing
problem: Zero-knowledge proofs (ZKP), especially zkSNARKs, remain computationally intensive for basic operations like matrix multiplication, requiring extensive constraint systems and creating significant overhead.
method: Proposes zkVC with optimized ZKP modules including Constraint-reduced Polynomial Circuit (CRPC) for reducing constraint overhead and Prefix-Sum Query (PSQ) for efficient aggregation; specializes in accelerating matrix multiplication proofs.
